en: The national flower, Sampaguita, releases its sweet fragrance at night to attract pollinating moths in the Philippine environment.
The Philippine eagle, our national bird, relies on old-growth dipterocarp forests to build its massive nests and hunt monkeys.
Ifugao farmers use stone walls in their rice terraces to prevent soil erosion and retain water for their crops.
Filipino scientist Angel Alcala pioneered coral reef transplantation to restore marine biodiversity in Philippine coastal environments.
The Panagbenga festival in Baguio celebrates the blooming of temperate plants like orchids and strawberries adapted to high altitudes.
The narra tree, the national tree, sheds its leaves during the dry season to conserve water in the Philippine climate.
Taal Volcano forms a unique lake-within-a-lake system where the main crater sits inside Taal Lake.
T'boli weavers extract strong fibers from the abaca plant stalks to dye and weave the traditional T'nalak cloth.
The carabao, our national animal, wallows in mud to lower its body temperature since it lacks sweat glands.
National scientist Gavino Trono studied seaweeds like carrageenan-producing Kappaphycus to boost the Philippine aquaculture industry.
Milkfish or bangus, the national fish, hatch in the ocean but migrate to shallow coastal lagoons to feed on algae.
Farmers in Lucban dry their harvested rice stalks under the sun to reduce moisture and prevent fungal growth before the Pahiyas festival.
